sections.label: Reading
sections.title: Equal Eligibility, Unequal Access
sections.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
The following municipality, program and observations are fictional. Arden offers a training grant to residents seeking a new qualification. Anyone meeting the same published income and residency criteria may apply. Officials initially describe the policy as equal access because the eligibility rule does not distinguish between neighborhoods. Yet application and completion patterns differ across the municipality. The available case notes report the difference without supplying a representative dataset or identifying its cause.

One explanation emphasizes individual choices: eligible residents may value the course differently or prefer immediate work. Another points to institutional conditions. Classes end after the last bus to two neighborhoods, some applicants lack reliable childcare, and the application requires documents from several offices. These mechanisms could constrain participation even where motivation is strong. Their plausibility, however, is not proof that they explain every non-application or withdrawal.

A proposed universal transport allowance would be simple to administer and avoid requiring participants to demonstrate exceptional need. Critics argue that some funds would go to people who already have adequate transport. A targeted package of evening transport and childcare support might direct more resources toward specific barriers, but it could introduce intrusive eligibility checks, administrative delays and errors that exclude people it is meant to help. A third proposal simplifies the application process for everyone, although simplification alone would not change the bus schedule.

The council must also decide what success means. More applications would show increased take-up, not necessarily qualification completion or lasting mobility. Higher completion among participants would be encouraging, but selection into the program could make a comparison with non-participants misleading. A credible evaluation would need a defensible comparison, attention to who remains excluded and a follow-up period suited to the outcome being claimed.

A balanced recommendation can therefore support action while remaining explicit about uncertainty. The absence of decisive causal evidence need not justify inaction, but neither does a plausible systemic explanation license certainty about a particular remedy. The policy should connect each intervention to an identified barrier, make its distributional choices visible and establish conditions for revision. Equal eligibility is a starting rule; whether it yields meaningful opportunity is an empirical and normative question.

items.prompt: Why does the case not establish the cause of different participation rates?
Give one mechanism that could restrict participation despite motivation.
What is the main administrative trade-off of targeting?
Why are more applications insufficient evidence of lasting mobility?

answers: Equal eligibility proves opportunity; unequal participation proves one systemic cause
People who join may differ from those who do not
Administrative simplicity versus more targeted support

sections.teacherNotes:
Teacher transcript:
I would resist two tempting conclusions about Arden’s training grant. One is that equal eligibility proves equal opportunity. The other is that unequal participation proves a single systemic cause. The case supports neither conclusion on its own. It gives us plausible mechanisms that deserve investigation, not a complete causal account.

My recommendation is to simplify the application for everyone while piloting evening transport where the timetable creates an identified barrier. Childcare support should also be considered, but its design needs consultation with prospective participants. We should record who cannot use each intervention and why.

Evaluation must distinguish take-up, completion and longer-term outcomes. An increase in applications would not, by itself, demonstrate social mobility. Nor would a higher completion rate among participants prove that the grant caused the difference, since people who join may differ from those who do not.

There is also a value judgment that evidence cannot make for us: how much administrative simplicity we are willing to exchange for more targeted support. That judgment should be stated openly. I would support a limited, reviewable policy with a clear comparison strategy, rather than promise a permanent solution before we understand the mechanisms. Uncertainty is a reason to design learning into the policy, not a reason to disguise assumptions as findings.

Read the questions aloud for young learners. Replay or reread in short sections if needed.

activity.title: A policy hearing with a written dissent
activity.objective: Write a nuanced policy analysis that separates causal hypotheses from evidence, weighs distributional trade-offs and specifies what would justify revision.
activity.materials:
Council group: Recommend a limited package using the fictional case only. State whose access improves and who may remain excluded.

Review group: Test the causal assumptions and administrative trade-offs. Do not treat a plausible mechanism as a measured effect.

Final task: Write a joint recommendation and a short dissent that accurately represents the strongest unresolved objection.

Form groups of 4 and model one short response.
Allow 18 minutes for preparation and practice; use the remaining time for responses and feedback.

Score each criterion 0–2: a qualified claim; accurate use of case evidence; a serious alternative explanation; an explicit trade-off; a justified revision condition. 8/10 indicates the task is substantially met. These are task rubrics, not formal CEFR certification.

value.title: Equal Eligibility, Unequal Access
value.purpose: Write a nuanced policy analysis that separates causal hypotheses from evidence, weighs distributional trade-offs and specifies what would justify revision.
value.instructions: Read for the situation, then use evidence to answer.
value.text:
The following municipality, program and observations are fictional. Arden offers a training grant to residents seeking a new qualification. Anyone meeting the same published income and residency criteria may apply. Officials initially describe the policy as equal access because the eligibility rule does not distinguish between neighborhoods. Yet application and completion patterns differ across the municipality. The available case notes report the difference without supplying a representative dataset or identifying its cause.

One explanation emphasizes individual choices: eligible residents may value the course differently or prefer immediate work. Another points to institutional conditions. Classes end after the last bus to two neighborhoods, some applicants lack reliable childcare, and the application requires documents from several offices. These mechanisms could constrain participation even where motivation is strong. Their plausibility, however, is not proof that they explain every non-application or withdrawal.

A proposed universal transport allowance would be simple to administer and avoid requiring participants to demonstrate exceptional need. Critics argue that some funds would go to people who already have adequate transport. A targeted package of evening transport and childcare support might direct more resources toward specific barriers, but it could introduce intrusive eligibility checks, administrative delays and errors that exclude people it is meant to help. A third proposal simplifies the application process for everyone, although simplification alone would not change the bus schedule.

The council must also decide what success means. More applications would show increased take-up, not necessarily qualification completion or lasting mobility. Higher completion among participants would be encouraging, but selection into the program could make a comparison with non-participants misleading. A credible evaluation would need a defensible comparison, attention to who remains excluded and a follow-up period suited to the outcome being claimed.

A balanced recommendation can therefore support action while remaining explicit about uncertainty. The absence of decisive causal evidence need not justify inaction, but neither does a plausible systemic explanation license certainty about a particular remedy. The policy should connect each intervention to an identified barrier, make its distributional choices visible and establish conditions for revision. Equal eligibility is a starting rule; whether it yields meaningful opportunity is an empirical and normative question.

value.title: The Evaluation Adviser’s Caution
value.purpose: Write a nuanced policy analysis that separates causal hypotheses from evidence, weighs distributional trade-offs and specifies what would justify revision.
value.instructions: Listen once for the situation and again for details.
value.script:
I would resist two tempting conclusions about Arden’s training grant. One is that equal eligibility proves equal opportunity. The other is that unequal participation proves a single systemic cause. The case supports neither conclusion on its own. It gives us plausible mechanisms that deserve investigation, not a complete causal account.

My recommendation is to simplify the application for everyone while piloting evening transport where the timetable creates an identified barrier. Childcare support should also be considered, but its design needs consultation with prospective participants. We should record who cannot use each intervention and why.

Evaluation must distinguish take-up, completion and longer-term outcomes. An increase in applications would not, by itself, demonstrate social mobility. Nor would a higher completion rate among participants prove that the grant caused the difference, since people who join may differ from those who do not.

There is also a value judgment that evidence cannot make for us: how much administrative simplicity we are willing to exchange for more targeted support. That judgment should be stated openly. I would support a limited, reviewable policy with a clear comparison strategy, rather than promise a permanent solution before we understand the mechanisms. Uncertainty is a reason to design learning into the policy, not a reason to disguise assumptions as findings.
